The primary advantage of DLC is that, because it directly coordinates EV charging load with electricity supply, it is guaranteed to lower overall electricity costs no matter how many vehicles participate. Its cost reductions can therefore serve as a benchmark for the cost reductions achieved by other coordination mechanisms at high EVMC participation levels. The disadvantages of DLC stem from the need to aggregate charging flexibility across many EVs to facilitate two-way communication between charging controls and grid operation software. Aggregation is necessary because grid operation software is designed to optimize hundreds to thousands of megawatt-scale devices. For example, FERC Order 2222 specifies a minimum aggregation size of 0.1 megawatt (MW) (Federal Energy Regulatory Commission [FERC] 2020), not thousands to millions of kilowatt-scale devices (i.e., EVs). Aggregation to present DLC to the bulk power system is challenging because of the requisite costs of software, communications, and controls, and the complications introduced by aggregation mathematics. Aggregation mathematics present an inherent challenge we find likely requires significantly reducing the flexibility of the aggregate resource offered to the bulk power system (Hale et al. 2022a), disadvantaging DLC. As an example, simply adding up the charging flexibility of all participating vehicles overstates aggregate flexibility by obscuring vehicle-level constraints that link the ability to accept charge (or not) with availability of a charger (or not). Any aggregation process that ignores this loss of information is likely to incorporate a significant degree of error in fulfilling aggregate load shift requests. Hao et al. (2013) show it is sometimes possible to bound aggregate flexibility with mathematical models that present either strictly less or strictly more flexibility than what is actually available. However, that method’s bounds are not tight enough to be practicable for multihour energy shifting (Hale et al. 2022b). Thus, this study, similar to Hale et al. (2022a), handles the aggregator’s information loss problem by discounting aggregate power and energy bounds to ensure aggregate dispatch requests can, with high probability, be fulfilled with low error. In summary, DLC’s disadvantages are increased cost of enabling two-way communication, increased computational complexity, and an inability to represent the full flexibility of individual EVs in megawatt-scale aggregations. Price-responsive dispatch mechanisms such as TOU and RTP have two primary advantages— ability to access an individual EV’s full scheduling flexibility and lower cost to implement than DLC—because they require only one-way communications and localized controls. Their primary disadvantage is that large quantities of price-responsive load can induce new and potentially costly-to-serve load spikes at times forecast to have low prices (Hale et al. 2022a).
